meta.title: The Praise Before the Ask
meta.subtitle: A closed dossier on flattery-then-ask sequencing — how it works, how to run it, and how to kill it when it's run on you
meta.description: Twelve cards on the oldest soft-power move in the room. Praise arrives first. The ask follows. Most people say yes before they notice the sequence. This file covers the anatomy, the deployment, the defense, the calibration, and what happens to trust when the move gets used too many times on the same person.

cards.title: Praise First, Then Ask
cards.hook: Every big ask works better after a compliment. The praise doesn't just soften them — it puts them in debt to you before the ask arrives.
cards.truth:
Most people think flattery just warms people up. That is the surface.
• Praise triggers the urge to give something back — the target feels owing before the ask lands.
• They move from neutral to grateful while you are still talking.
• The trap: they say yes to the ask to pay off the good feeling, not because the ask is good.
cards.remember: Give them something to feel good about. Then ask.
cards.theySee: A person telling them they did great work right before making a request.

signals.t: They lead with how great you are before they get to the point at all.
Someone who is normally flat suddenly sounds very enthusiastic toward you.
They stop after the compliment and wait, as if letting it settle before continuing.
Within two sentences of the praise, a request appears.

steps.title: Pick a real strength
steps.desc: Name one thing they actually did well. Invented praise reads as fake immediately and kills the setup before the ask arrives.

steps.title: Let the praise breathe
steps.desc: Say the compliment, then pause three seconds. Let them feel it before you say another word.

steps.title: Make the ask in one sentence
steps.desc: State what you need plainly. No hedging. The warm-up is finished — the ask stands or falls on its own now.

cards.script: "That report you put together for the board was cleaner than anything I've seen this quarter — I want to ask you something."
cards.counter:
Watch for praise that arrives just before a request — the timing is the tell.
• Notice if you feel suddenly warm toward the person right as they are about to ask.
• Say 'Thanks — what do you need?' and name the ask first to break the flow.
• Judge the request on its own cost, not on how the compliment made you feel.
cards.insight: The move works best the first few times. Run it on the same person repeatedly and you train them to expect an ask after every compliment — and the praise stops being worth anything.

cards.title: Label the Identity You Need Them to Live Up To
cards.hook: Compliments don't just feel good. They change what the person is willing to do next by telling them who they are.
cards.truth:
The praised person stops analyzing the ask and starts acting like the person you just described.
• Being called skilled at something makes them want to prove they are that person.
• They tie their sense of self to the label and feel pressure to stay consistent with it.
• The trap: they accept harder asks than they normally would just to avoid contradicting the identity you gave them.
cards.remember: Name the identity you want them to live up to. Then ask.
cards.theySee: Someone telling them they are exactly the kind of person who is good at the thing being asked for.

signals.t: They call you the best at this or the only one who gets it before naming what they want.
They use your name more than once in a short span, pulling your attention before the ask.
The compliment matches exactly the skill or trait the ask requires from you.
After the praise, they pause and look at you as if the answer is already obvious.

steps.title: Name the specific identity first
steps.desc: Say the exact thing they are good at — 'You are the sharpest negotiator on this team' — before anything else.

steps.title: Link the label directly to the ask
steps.desc: Connect the skill you named to what you need — 'That is exactly why I need you on this call.'

steps.title: Stay quiet after asking
steps.desc: Say nothing after the request. Let the identity pressure do the work. Silence here is the move.

cards.script: "You are the only person on this team who can actually read a room — I need you in that client meeting tomorrow at 2."
cards.counter:
When praise matches a request too precisely, slow down — that fit is not a coincidence.
• Check if the compliment names exactly the skill the ask requires.
• Ask yourself if you would say yes to the same request from a stranger with no warm-up.
• Separate how the praise made you feel from what the ask actually costs you.
cards.insight: The stronger the identity label, the harder it is to say no without feeling like a fraud — and that is exactly where this move gets sharp enough to cut both ways.

cards.title: Spot the Flattery Setup Before the Ask Lands
cards.hook: The ask is visible three sentences before it arrives. By the time they get there, you have already been moved.
cards.truth:
Most people only notice the ask. They miss the setup entirely because they are inside the warm feeling when it counts.
• The setup always involves a shift in tone — from neutral to warm, or from distant to close.
• The time between praise and ask is almost always under one minute.
• The trap: if you notice it late, the warmth has already landed and the ask has momentum you did not choose to give it.
cards.remember: Watch for warmth that shows up right before someone needs something.
cards.theySee: A colleague who is usually brief suddenly being generous with compliments and personal attention.

signals.t: Their voice or message gets noticeably warmer than it was moments before.
They skip normal chat and go straight to a compliment — unusual behavior for them.
They hold eye contact deliberately while giving the compliment, more than they normally would.
The compliment comes out too smoothly, as if they planned it before the conversation started.

steps.title: Note the baseline first
steps.desc: In any ongoing relationship, keep track of how this person normally talks to you. The shift from that normal is the signal — not the praise itself.

steps.title: Name the pattern silently
steps.desc: When the warm-up hits, say to yourself: 'They want something.' Do not say it out loud. Hold it, and wait for the ask.

steps.title: Let the full sequence play out before you react
steps.desc: Hear the ask completely before showing any reaction. You learn more from the ask than from the praise. Do not tip your hand early.

cards.script: "I appreciate that — what is it you're looking to get done?"
cards.counter:
If someone spots your setup, they will deflect the compliment and push you straight to the ask.
• Watch for the target cutting your praise short with a direct question.
• If that happens, name the ask immediately — stalling now reads as manipulation.
• Do not try to re-run the warm-up. One attempt, then go direct.
cards.insight: Spotting the setup does not protect you on its own. Knowing what they are about to ask tells you far more than the praise ever will — because the ask reveals what they think your yes is worth.

cards.title: Spot the Group Warm-Up Before a Mass Ask
cards.hook: Some people do not flatter one person. They flatter the whole room — then ask the whole room for something.
cards.truth:
Group flattery is harder to resist because no one wants to be the person who breaks a warm mood.
• When a whole room feels good at once, individual resistance drops — no one wants to look cold.
• The asker spreads credit broadly and collects agreement broadly in the same move.
• The trap: in a group, saying no feels like you are the only person unmoved, and that social pressure does most of the work.
cards.remember: When everyone gets praised at once, check what is about to be asked of everyone.
cards.theySee: A person in a meeting who spends five minutes complimenting the whole team before putting the real agenda item on the table.

signals.t: Generic compliments go to every person in the room — no specifics, but everyone feels included.
You can feel the group relax and lean forward together after the praise begins.
The speaker makes deliberate eye contact with each person during the warm-up sequence.
The request comes framed as 'all of us' or 'the team' — designed to feel like a collective choice.

steps.title: Stay flat while others warm up
steps.desc: When a room lifts fast under flattery, keep your own reaction neutral. Note who else stays flat — those are your allies if you need to push back on the ask.

steps.title: Write down the ask word-for-word as it is made
steps.desc: Physically writing the request separates it from the warm feeling in the room and makes it easier to evaluate on its own.

steps.title: Ask one clarifying question before anyone agrees
steps.desc: Say 'What does this require from each person specifically over the next two weeks?' — it forces the asker to be concrete and breaks the group agreement before it sets.

cards.script: "Before we commit — what exactly does this require from each of us in the next two weeks?"
cards.counter:
If someone breaks the group warmth with a hard question, others wake up fast — prepare for that.
• Have a specific answer ready for what the ask costs each person individually.
• Do not try to re-warm the room after a cold question — it reads as panic.
• Name the benefit to the individuals directly, not just the group as a whole.
cards.insight: The person who asks the first clarifying question in a warmed-up room holds more power than the person who ran the warm-up — they just reset who is in control of the frame.

cards.title: Match Your Praise to the Size of What You Are Asking For
cards.hook: A small compliment before a big ask does not work. The mismatch tells them you do not value what you are requesting — and the ask fails.
cards.truth:
The praise and the ask need to feel like they are in the same weight class or the whole sequence reads as cheap.
• A light compliment before a heavy ask signals that you undervalue what you are requesting.
• Too much praise before a small ask creates suspicion that something bigger is coming.
• The trap: calibrating poorly does not just hurt this ask — it makes the target suspicious of every future compliment you give them.
cards.remember: Big ask needs big praise. Small ask, small praise. Never the other way.
cards.theySee: A manager giving a short 'nice job' and then immediately asking someone to take on a full new project alone.

signals.t: The compliment is vague or one sentence long right before a large, costly request.
They sit with the compliment too long, as if building up to something massive.
The request is noticeably larger than what the amount of praise would suggest is coming.
Their face changes when they hear the ask — the mismatch between praise and request registers visibly.

steps.title: Size the ask first, not the praise
steps.desc: Before you plan what to say, pin down exactly how big the ask is in time, money, or effort. That number sets your praise budget.

steps.title: Match praise effort to ask effort
steps.desc: Small ask: one genuine sentence. Medium ask: two sentences plus a specific example of their work. Big ask: a detailed, personal compliment they have not heard before from anyone.

steps.title: Rehearse the transition line
steps.desc: Write the sentence that connects your compliment to your ask. Say it out loud once before the real conversation so it sounds natural, not constructed.

cards.script: "The way you handled the vendor contract last month — that kind of judgment is exactly what this next negotiation needs. I want you leading it."
cards.counter:
When praise and ask feel mismatched in size, trust the mismatch — it tells you the asker has not thought through what they are really asking.
• Notice if the compliment feels too big or too small for the actual request that follows.
• Ask them to break the ask into smaller parts so you can see the real cost.
• Do not let good praise make you accept a poorly scoped request.
cards.insight: The person who calibrates praise well looks like they thought about you. The person who over-praises looks desperate. Both readings happen before the ask is even finished — and the target decides which one you are before they answer.

cards.title: Run the Sequence on Decision-Makers, Not Just Peers
cards.hook: Most people run flattery moves sideways — on colleagues. The real payoff is up the chain, where one yes changes everything.
cards.truth:
Decision-makers hear praise constantly — generic flattery does not move them because they are already saturated with it.
• Specific praise about a hard call they made under pressure cuts through because it is rare.
• When a senior person feels seen for a difficult decision, they want to prove that judgment was right — by backing your ask.
• The trap: praise their power or their title and they smell the move. Praise the specific choice they made and they do not.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 24 — Play the Perfect Courtier
cards.remember: Do not praise who they are. Praise one specific call they made.
cards.theySee: A subordinate who brings up a real decision the boss made months ago, names the result, and then makes a narrow focused request.

signals.t: The person references a specific past decision of yours by name or context before stating what they need.
They mention an actual measurable result from that decision, not just that it was a good one.
The request is small and specific — not an open-ended blank-check ask.
They come to you alone — not in front of a group where it would read as performance.

steps.title: Find one real call they made that worked
steps.desc: Look back three to six months. Find a specific decision this person made that had a clear, measurable result. Write it in one sentence before the conversation.

steps.title: State the decision and the result plainly
steps.desc: Open with that one sentence. Do not editorialize or add warmth on top. Let the fact land before you say anything else.

steps.title: Make a narrow, specific ask
steps.desc: Ask for one concrete thing — a signature, a name, an introduction. Not a broad request. Narrow asks close faster after specific praise than open ones do.

cards.script: "The call you made to hold the pricing in Q3 — that's the reason we kept three accounts. I need your sign-off on a similar hold for the Henderson deal."
cards.counter:
Senior people who hear oddly specific praise from someone junior should ask themselves: what does this person need right now?
• Notice if the compliment is specific enough that it required preparation — that tells you the ask was planned.
• Slow down before agreeing. The more precise the praise, the more thought went into what follows.
• Ask them to put the request in writing before you give an answer.
cards.insight: The decision-maker who gets praised for a hard call often wants to repeat it — and your ask gives them the vehicle. The harder move is knowing when their past call was wrong and making the ask anyway.

cards.title: Run It on the Peer Who Controls Access
cards.hook: The person blocking you is not always the boss. Sometimes it is the colleague with the calendar, the list, or the room key.
cards.truth:
Peers with gate-keeping roles almost never get praised for the gate-keeping itself — most people ignore it and just take what they need.
• Naming what they actually do — manage the flow, keep the schedule running — is unusual and hits them differently than generic praise.
• When a peer feels seen for unglamorous work, they become willing to bend the normal rules slightly for you.
• The trap: praise them in front of others and it reads as performance. Do it one-on-one and it reads as real.
cards.remember: Praise the boring job they do that nobody else notices.
cards.theySee: A colleague stopping by their desk alone, naming something specific about how they run the process, before asking for a small favor with access or scheduling.

signals.t: They come to you when you are alone, not in a meeting or group setting.
They name your actual workflow or administrative function specifically rather than just saying good job.
The request is modest — an earlier slot, a name added to a list, a door opened.
They do not pressure you — they plant the ask and wait for you to respond at your own pace.

steps.title: Name the unglamorous work first
steps.desc: Say exactly what they do that no one mentions — 'You are the one who keeps the vendor list current and nobody acknowledges that.'

steps.title: Pause long enough for them to respond
steps.desc: After naming it, stop talking. Let them say something. This is not a monologue — their response tells you the praise landed.

steps.title: Ask for one small, specific thing
steps.desc: Keep the ask low-cost for them. 'Can you add me to the Thursday slot?' Not 'Can you rearrange the whole schedule?'

cards.script: "You're the only one who actually keeps the vendor contact list clean — everyone just uses it and never says anything. Can you add the Westfield contact before Thursday?"
cards.counter:
When a peer compliments your workflow before asking for access, they want the gate opened.
• Appreciate the recognition but treat the ask as entirely separate from the compliment.
• If the ask is outside your normal process, say so clearly — 'I would need approval to do that.'
• Do not over-deliver just because someone finally noticed your work.
cards.insight: Gate-keepers who get praised start thinking of themselves as important rather than just busy — and that shift makes them more helpful over time, not just once. You have changed how they see the role, not just how they see you.

cards.title: Recognize When the Praise Is Designed to Lock You In
cards.hook: You are in the middle of agreeing before you notice you were set up. The good feeling did its job before the ask even arrived.
cards.truth:
Being flattered shifts your goal from evaluating the ask to staying consistent with the praise.
• Once you accept the compliment, turning down the ask feels like denying the identity they gave you.
• The sequence is fast — praise, ask, your yes — and the pause to think feels socially wrong in the moment.
• The trap: saying no after accepting flattery triggers guilt, not analysis, and guilt is much harder to think through.
cards.principle: Cialdini: Commitment and Consistency — Identity Trap
cards.remember: A good compliment does not mean a good ask. Separate the two every time.
cards.theySee: A person nodding along happily to praise, then looking flustered when they realize they are already halfway to agreeing.

signals.t: A quick surge of good feeling hits you right before they state what they want.
The praise names exactly the skill or trait the request is about to require from you.
Any hesitation on your part feels socially awkward in the moment — that feeling was installed.
You catch yourself agreeing with your body before you have consciously decided anything.

steps.title: Name the sequence to yourself the moment the warm-up starts
steps.desc: Say silently: 'Praise. Ask is coming.' This one internal sentence breaks the automatic path from feeling warm to saying yes.

steps.title: Accept the compliment, then stop talking
steps.desc: Say 'Thank you' and stay quiet. Do not let the thank-you carry momentum into agreement. Two seconds of silence re-sets your position.

steps.title: Judge the ask alone, without the praise
steps.desc: Ask yourself: if a stranger made this exact request with zero warm-up, would I say yes? If the answer is no, the flattery was doing the work, not the ask.

cards.script: "I appreciate that — let me think about it and get back to you by tomorrow."
cards.counter:
This card is the defense itself — the counter is catching yourself justifying a weak yes with the compliment they gave you.
• Notice when you are telling yourself 'they said something nice, I should help.'
• That feeling is the sequence running automatically. Stop it at that sentence.
• Give your actual answer, not the one that maintains the warm feeling between you.
cards.insight: The fastest sign this is happening to you is the urge to decide immediately. That urgency is not yours — it was put there by the warm-up. The ask that needs an answer right now almost never does.

cards.title: Stall the Ask Without Wrecking the Relationship
cards.hook: You have spotted the setup but cannot say no cleanly yet. The move is to buy time without showing them you have seen through it.
cards.truth:
Saying no immediately after praise can feel sharp and push the other person into a defensive position.
• A timed delay gives you space to decide and gives them the impression you are taking them seriously.
• The relationship stays intact because you have not rejected them — you have only moved the timeline.
• The trap: too long a delay and they will re-run the warm-up sequence when they come back, which now reads as obvious.
cards.remember: Slow down the ask without killing the goodwill. Buy yourself one day.
cards.theySee: A person who smiles, thanks them genuinely, and names a specific time they will respond — not a vague maybe later.

signals.t: You have not had time to think through what saying yes actually costs you in time or exposure.
You cannot tell yet whether the ask is good for you independent of how the praise made you feel.
A hard no right now would damage something worth keeping over time.
They have not said when they need an answer — you have more room than their urgency implies.

steps.title: Accept the compliment warmly and briefly
steps.desc: Say 'Thank you — that means something' and stop. Do not fill the silence that follows with more words.

steps.title: Name a specific time to respond
steps.desc: Say 'I want to give this proper thought — I will come back to you by Thursday afternoon.' Specific time, not 'I will think about it.'

steps.title: Use the time to decide on the actual merits
steps.desc: In the next 24 hours, write down what saying yes costs you. Then decide on that, not on how the compliment felt.

cards.script: "I appreciate you saying that — I want to give this real thought. I'll come back to you by Thursday afternoon."
cards.counter:
When someone stalls after your sequence, the praise worked but the ask did not land cleanly.
• Do not re-run the warm-up when they come back — it makes the pattern visible.
• Let the stall play out and return with a smaller or more specific ask.
• Or ask them directly what would make the ask easier to say yes to.
cards.insight: The person who asks for time after being praised is not neutral — they spotted something. When they come back, their answer is already decided. The only question is how they plan to deliver the no.

cards.title: Flatter Back and Make Your Own Ask First
cards.hook: They opened with praise to soften you. You can praise them back immediately — and use that to reset who is asking whom.
cards.truth:
Matching praise with praise before naming your own ask flips the position completely.
• Now both of you have given something. The urge to give back runs both ways.
• The person who makes the second ask has more information — they know what the other person wants.
• The trap: if you praise back too quickly it looks reactive and deliberate. Wait one beat before returning it.
cards.remember: Match their praise, then make your own ask before they make theirs.
cards.theySee: Someone who accepts their compliment graciously, gives a sincere one back, and then names what they need before the original asker can get to their own request.

signals.t: They smile and accept your compliment — they are now in give-back mode too.
After your praise they stop, no longer sure who is asking whom.
The conversation tone shifts — you are no longer just the target of their sequence.
They lose the flow of their own warm-up while processing the compliment you just returned.

steps.title: Accept their compliment in one sentence and stop
steps.desc: Say 'Thank you, I appreciate that' and go quiet. Do not elaborate or deflect the praise.

steps.title: Give a specific compliment back immediately
steps.desc: Name one real thing they have done well — not a vague mirror, a specific action you actually observed. This breaks the momentum of their setup.

steps.title: Make your ask before they make theirs
steps.desc: While they are still processing the returned praise, state your request plainly. You now hold the position of asker rather than target.

cards.script: "I really appreciate that — and honestly, the way you handled the Eastbrook meeting was sharp work. While I have you — I need your help on something."
cards.counter:
If someone absorbs your flattery and immediately praises you back before making an ask, you have lost the position.
• Notice the move: they returned warmth and jumped to a request before you could.
• Acknowledge their ask but name your own before you answer theirs.
• Now you are both in a trade. Drop the flattery and name what you actually want.
cards.insight: Two people running this sequence on each other at the same time stops being persuasion and becomes a negotiation. The one who names a concrete trade first wins — and the one who keeps adding praise loses ground with every sentence.

cards.title: Over-Praising Before an Ask Signals Desperation
cards.hook: Load up too much praise and the ask dies before you make it. They start wondering what you really want before they have even heard the request.
cards.truth:
Excessive praise before an ask creates suspicion faster than no praise at all.
• Multiple compliments in a row tell the target something large is coming — their defense goes up.
• The more praise stacks up, the more the ask feels like a debt collection when it finally arrives.
• The trap: over-praising once teaches them your pattern and every future compliment now reads as a setup before you have said a word.
cards.remember: Three compliments in a row is too many. One is usually enough.
cards.theySee: A person who has received four compliments in two minutes from someone who normally gives none, now waiting with visible tension for the real point.

signals.t: You have given two praises already and still have not made the ask — you are stacking too many.
Their body closes slightly — arms in, eye contact dropping — in the middle of your compliments.
A slow 'okay' or 'right...' mid-praise means they are waiting for the other shoe to drop.
You are adding more praise because you are afraid the ask will fail — and they can feel that anxiety.

steps.title: Write your one compliment before the conversation
steps.desc: One sentence only. Write it down. That is all the praise you are allowed before the ask. No second sentence, no 'and also.'

steps.title: Deliver it and move directly to the ask
steps.desc: Say the compliment. Then transition immediately — 'Here is what I need.' No second compliment. No filler sentence that buys time.

steps.title: If you catch yourself adding more praise mid-conversation, stop
steps.desc: Cut the extra praise off and go to the ask. Stopping mid-pile is less damaging than finishing it.

cards.script: "You ran that handoff well last month — here's what I need from you on the next one."
cards.counter:
When someone gives you an unusual volume of praise, the ask that follows is going to be large.
• Count the compliments. More than two in a row and you are being softened for something significant.
• Ask them directly: 'What are you building up to?' Most people will go to the ask faster when named.
• Let the ask land fully before you respond — not before.
cards.insight: The person who can make the ask after one clean compliment has more confidence than the person who needs four. That gap shows before the ask is finished — and it affects the answer before you have said what you want.

cards.title: Run the Sequence Too Often and Every Compliment Becomes Suspect
cards.hook: Run flattery-then-ask on the same person three times. After that, every compliment you give them reads as an invoice — including the ones that are real.
cards.truth:
The sequence has a shelf life. Run it past the limit and you lose the tool with that person for good.
• Once the pattern is visible, the target pre-assigns all your future praise as the setup to a request.
• They stop feeling the compliment and start waiting for what you want.
• The trap: you have trained them to distrust praise itself — now even genuine compliments get rejected before they land.
cards.remember: Use it sparingly. Every repeat makes the next compliment worth less with that person.
cards.theySee: A person who used to respond warmly to compliments from you but now just looks at you flatly and waits for the ask.

signals.t: They do not respond to your praise at all — they just wait in silence for what comes next.
They say 'okay, what do you need?' before you have made any ask at all.
The warmth you used to generate with praise no longer appears on their face or in their response.

signals.l: They avoid being alone with you
signals.t: They find reasons not to be in one-on-one situations — they do not want to be run through the sequence again.

steps.title: Count how many times you have run this on one person
steps.desc: If it is more than twice in 90 days with the same person, you are close to the limit. Stop and wait.

steps.title: Give genuine praise with no ask attached
steps.desc: Compliment them on something real and then end the conversation. Nothing follows. Rebuild the signal so praise means something again.

steps.title: When the next ask is real, make it without a warm-up
steps.desc: State the ask directly and let it stand on its own. A direct ask reads as more trustworthy than a warm-up ask once someone has seen the pattern.

cards.script: "I just wanted to say the way you handled that client last week was genuinely good. That's it — nothing else."
cards.counter:
If a person's compliments make you wait for what they want, you have correctly read the pattern.
• Name it plainly: 'What do you need?' and let them be direct with you.
• If they say there is no ask — just a compliment — reset slowly. Trust does not rebuild in one conversation.
• Watch whether they start giving uncoupled praise over time. That is the repair move, and it takes weeks.
cards.insight: The highest cost of running this sequence too often is not that the asks start failing — it is that you lose the ability to give that person a genuine compliment ever again. Some tools only survive if you use them rarely enough that the other person never learns the name for what you are doing.
